---
title: "Exporting results"
---

The frame `run_scenarios` returns does not travel as it stands, because two of its columns hold
NumPy arrays rather than numbers, and an array written into a CSV cell comes back as text. The
scalars and the trajectories need separate files. We write the scalar summary to one CSV, stack
the trajectories into a long table, and read both back in R.

The grid is the same five arms built in [A scenario grid](scenario-grid.qmd), rebuilt from the
same district dictionary.

```{python}
import pathlib

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from estimint import run_scenarios, preload_models
from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget

district = dict(
    res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0,
    py_only=0.70, routine=0.0,
    eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"),
)

grid = [
    Scenario(name="Withdraw", **district),
    Scenario(name="Pyrethroid-only", itn_future=0.70,
             net_type_future="pyrethroid_only", **district),
    Scenario(name="PBO", itn_future=0.70,
             net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", **district),
    Scenario(name="Pyrrole", itn_future=0.70,
             net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole", **district),
    Scenario(name="PBO + IRS + LSM", itn_future=0.70,
             net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, **district),
]

res = run_scenarios(grid)
```

## An output directory

`pathlib` is Python's path library. A `Path` is an object rather than a string, one that composes
with the `/` operator and can make its own directory on disk.

```{python}
outputs = pathlib.Path("outputs")
outputs.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

outputs.resolve()
```

`exist_ok=True` makes the call idempotent, so the cell can be re-run without raising on the second
pass. Paths resolve against the working directory of the session rather than the file the code
sits in, and under Quarto that directory is the project root, so `outputs/` lands at the top of
the project. `resolve()` prints the absolute path, which is worth reading before a long run starts
writing into it.

## The scalar summary

Twenty-one of the twenty-three columns are scalars, and those are the ones that belong in a
spreadsheet. Drop the other two first.

```{python}
summary = res.drop(columns=["prevalence", "cases"])
summary.to_csv(outputs / "summary.csv", index=False)

pd.read_csv(outputs / "summary.csv")[
    ["name", "net_future", "dn0_future", "eir_baseline", "prev_endline", "cases_endline"]
]
```

`index=False` suppresses pandas' row numbers, which are an artefact of the frame rather than data
and would otherwise arrive in R as a nameless leading column. Read the file straight back. It is
the only way to find that a column expected to be numeric has come back as text.

## Array columns in a CSV

`to_csv` takes an array column without complaint and writes the array's text representation into
the cell, which is the string that printing the array would produce, brackets and line breaks
included.

```{python}
res.to_csv(outputs / "summary-broken.csv", index=False)

broken = pd.read_csv(outputs / "summary-broken.csv")
cell = broken.loc[0, "prevalence"]

type(cell), len(cell), cell[:60]
```

What comes back is a single string some 1,700 characters long rather than the 157 numbers that
went in. Note that no error is raised. The file is valid CSV, the column is text from then on, and
anything downstream either fails on it or silently skips it. In R, `read_csv` types it as `chr`
and moves on.

The array is not truncated, because NumPy elides only arrays above a thousand elements and 157 is
below that threshold, so every number the emulator produced is present, embedded in a single
string with newlines running through it. Recovering them means parsing that string. Drop the array
columns before writing instead.

```{python}
(outputs / "summary-broken.csv").unlink()
```

## Tidy format

The trajectories want their own file in long form, one row per scenario per timestep, which is the
shape `ggplot2` and `dplyr` expect. Recover the time grid from the emulator, then stack the
arrays.

```{python}
_, artifacts = preload_models()
cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config

n_steps = cfg["n_steps"]
abs_t = cfg["model_start_day"] + cfg["window_size"] * np.arange(n_steps)
years = (abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]) / 365

trajectories = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "name": np.repeat(res["name"].to_numpy(), n_steps),
        "day": np.tile(abs_t, len(res)),
        "years": np.tile(years, len(res)),
        "prevalence": np.concatenate(res["prevalence"].to_list()),
        "cases": np.concatenate(res["cases"].to_list()),
    }
)

trajectories.shape
```

`np.repeat` gives each scenario name 157 consecutive rows, `np.tile` repeats the time grid once
per scenario, and `np.concatenate` on the list of arrays flattens them in the same order. Five
scenarios of 157 windows is 785 rows.

```{python}
trajectories.head()
```

Keeping both `day` and `years` costs one column and saves an argument later. `day` is the model's
own clock and is what you would join on, while `years` is centred on the campaign and is what you
plot against.

```{python}
trajectories.to_csv(outputs / "trajectories.csv", index=False)

sorted(p.name for p in outputs.iterdir())
```

## Reading the files in R

Both files are plain CSV with a header row. Nothing about them is Python-specific.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

summary <- read_csv("outputs/summary.csv")
traj <- read_csv("outputs/trajectories.csv")

summary |>
  select(name, net_future, dn0_future, prev_endline, cases_endline) |>
  arrange(prev_endline)

ggplot(traj, aes(x = years, y = prevalence, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Years since campaign", y = "Prevalence (under 5)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

`read_csv` types the columns from the data, so `name` is a character vector and everything else a
double. The `years` column puts the campaign at zero, which makes
`geom_vline(xintercept = 0)` the R equivalent of the dashed campaign rule on the matplotlib
figures. For a longer-lived pipeline, prefer Parquet, with `trajectories.to_parquet()` on the
Python side and `arrow::read_parquet()` on the R side, which preserves the dtypes exactly and
produces smaller files into the bargain. A number cannot come back as text.
